objectives: Say what the Sun, the Moon and a star each are.
Tell a planet apart from a star.
Explain why the Moon seems to change shape during a month.
Find the Big Dipper and Orion in the night sky.
Use the words orbit, light and eclipse correctly.
Stay safe when you look at the Sun.

sections.body:
The sky looks full of lights. But the lights are not all the same kind of thing.

The **Sun** is a star. It is a huge ball of hot gas. A million Earths could fit inside it. It makes its own light, and that light reaches us in about eight minutes.

The **Moon** is not a star. It is a ball of rock that goes around the Earth. The Moon has no light of its own. The light we see on it is sunlight that the Moon bounces back to us.

A **star** is a ball of hot gas that makes its own light. The Sun is our nearest star. Many other stars are so far away that they look like tiny dots.

A **planet** is different. A planet is a big ball that goes around a star. It has no light of its own. Earth is a planet. So are Mars, Jupiter and Saturn.

So the sky holds three kinds of lights. Stars shine by themselves. Planets and moons shine by reflected light. The Sun is special, because it is a star that is close enough for us to feel its warmth.
examples: The Sun is a star, and it is the closest one to Earth.
The Moon has no light of its own.
A planet is a big ball that goes around a star.
sections.heading: What the Sun, the Moon and the Stars Are

sections.body:
Everything alive on Earth depends on the Sun. Plants use its light to make their food. We eat the plants, or the animals that eat the plants.

The Sun also sends out heat. This heat keeps the Earth warm enough for water to stay liquid. Without it, our oceans would freeze solid.

The Sun is not a campfire. It does not burn like wood burns. Deep inside it, hydrogen turns into helium, and that releases an enormous amount of energy.

That energy takes a long time to travel out. It leaves the surface as light, and it takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.

Light from the Sun warms the ground, and the ground warms the air above it. That is why a sunny day is warmer at your feet than high up in the air.

The Sun is gentle when it warms the sky. It is dangerous when you look straight at it.
examples: Plants use sunlight to make their food.
The Sun's light takes eight minutes to reach us.
The ground warms the air above it on a sunny day.
sections.heading: Why the Sun Gives Us Light and Heat

sections.body:
The Moon does not really change shape. Its shape stays the same all the time.

But the Moon goes around the Earth, once a month. As it moves, we see different parts of its sunlit half.

Sometimes we see nearly all of the lit half. That is a **full moon**. The Moon looks big and round and bright.

Sometimes we see only a thin bright slice. That is a **crescent moon**, and you can see it in the evening sky.

Sometimes the lit part is on the side, so we see half of it. That is a **half moon**.

Sometimes the lit part faces away from us, so we cannot see it at all. That is a **new moon**, and the sky around it looks very dark.

This whole pattern is called the **phases of the moon**. It takes about 29 days to finish one round.

Sometimes the Moon passes right in front of the Sun. That is a **solar eclipse**, and the day turns dark for a few minutes. You can only watch it safely with special eclipse glasses.
examples: The Moon does not change shape, we only see different parts of it.
A full moon looks big and round and bright.
A crescent moon is the thin bright slice in the evening sky.
sections.heading: Why the Moon Seems to Change Shape

sections.body:
You do not need a telescope to see stars. You need a dark sky, a little patience, and to know where to look.

Step outside on a clear night. Turn off the lights first. The darker the sky, the more stars you can see.

Let your eyes get used to the dark. It takes a few minutes. Then look up.

Find the Big Dipper. It is seven bright stars in a shape like a ladle. Follow the two stars at the end of the ladle, and you will find the North Star.

Look for three bright stars in a straight line in the middle of the sky. That is Orion. The middle star looks like a belt, and below it there are two bright stars.

Stay out for fifteen minutes without looking at your phone. Your eyes will notice more and more stars.

If you look at the same patch of sky every month, you will see it turn. The stars rise a little later each night as the months go by.
examples: The sky is darker here, so I can see more stars.
I followed the ladle and found the North Star.
That straight line of three stars is Orion.
sections.heading: How to Watch the Night Sky
steps: Go outside on a clear night and turn off the lights.
Wait a few minutes for your eyes to get used to the dark.
Find the Big Dipper, seven stars in a ladle shape.
Follow the two end stars of the ladle to the North Star.
Look for the three stars of Orion and the belt in the middle.
Stay out for fifteen minutes without looking at your phone.

sections.body:
These are the words you will need when you talk about the sky.

A **star** is a ball of hot gas that makes its own light. The Sun is a star.

A **planet** is a big ball that goes around a star and shines only with borrowed light.

A **moon** is a ball of rock that goes around a planet. Our Moon goes around the Earth.

To **orbit** means to go around and around. The Moon orbits the Earth, and the Earth orbits the Sun.

**Light** is what lets us see. Stars make their own light, and everything else bounces it back.

**Eclipse** is the word for when one body hides another. In a solar eclipse, the Moon hides the Sun.
sections.heading: The Words We Use for the Sky

terms.example: That bright dot is a star, shining all by itself.

terms.gloss: A big ball that goes around a star. It has no light of its own.

terms.example: The Moon goes around the Earth once a month.
terms.gloss: A ball of rock that goes around a planet and shows us the light it bounces back.

terms.example: We wore eclipse glasses to watch the eclipse safely.
terms.gloss: When one space object hides another. In a solar eclipse, the Moon hides the Sun.

sections.body:
Never look straight at the Sun. Not with your naked eye, not with binoculars, and not through a camera or a telescope. The Sun is so bright that it can burn the part of your eye that makes an image. This can happen in a few seconds, and the damage may never heal.

If you want to see the Sun, ask an adult to help you make a **pinhole projector**. Make a tiny hole in a card. Point the card at the Sun. Let the sunlight come through the hole and land on a white sheet of paper. Then you can look at the picture on the paper, safely.

Never wear ordinary sunglasses to look at the Sun. Dark glasses make it worse, because your pupils stay wide open and let in more light.

For an eclipse, use eclipse glasses. They are made of a special dark film that blocks almost all the Sun's light. Ordinary sunglasses are not eclipse glasses.

If the sky is cloudy, just wait for a clear day. It is not worth the risk.
sections.heading: Looking at the Sun Safely

item.summary: The sky is full of lights, but they are not all the same kind of thing. After reading this, you can say what the Sun, the Moon and a star each are, explain why the Moon seems to change shape, and find real stars in the night sky without a telescope.
